content: Longitudinal waves are a type of wave in which the oscillations or vibrations of the particles in the medium occur in the same direction as the wave's propagation. This means that the motion of the particles is parallel to the direction in which the wave travels. Mechanical longitudinal waves are also referred to as compressional waves or compression waves. Non-Electromagnetic Longitudinal Waves Non-electromagnetic longitudinal waves include sound waves and seismic P-waves. Seismic P-waves, on the other hand, are generated by events such as earthquakes or explosions and travel through the Earth's interior. Sound Waves For longitudinal harmonic sound waves, their frequency and wavelength can be mathematically described. The displacement of particles from their equilibrium position in the direction of wave propagation is denoted as ( y(x,t) ). Here: ( x ) represents the distance from the wave source to the point of interest. ( t ) is the elapsed time. ( y_0 ) is the amplitude of the oscillations. ( c ) is the speed of the wave. ( omega ) is the angular frequency of the wave. The term ( x/c ) represents the time it takes for the wave to travel a distance ( x ). In this case: ( y_0 ) is the amplitude of displacement. ( k ) is the wave number. ( x ) is the distance along the propagation axis. ( omega ) is the angular frequency. ( t ) is time. ( phi ) is the phase difference. The restoring force that brings the medium back to its original position is determined by the medium's bulk modulus. Electromagnetic Longitudinal Waves Maxwell's equations predict the existence of electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, which are transverse in nature. In transverse waves, the electric and magnetic fields oscillate perpendicularly to the direction of wave propagation. However, in certain conditions, such as in plasmas or confined spaces, electromagnetic waves can exhibit longitudinal characteristics, or a combination of longitudinal and transverse properties. In plasmas, longitudinal waves can occur under specific conditions, such as in force-free magnetic fields. Historically, there was debate regarding the existence of longitudinal electromagnetic waves in a vacuum. Helmholtz's theory initially suggested their possibility, but Oliver Heaviside later concluded that longitudinal electromagnetic waves do not exist in free space or homogeneous media. However, longitudinal waves can arise at the interface between different media, such as at the boundary between layers of the Earth's atmosphere and its surface, or in phenomena like the Schumann resonance. Maxwell's equations also allow for the existence of longitudinal waves in certain guided wave systems or plasma environments. These waves are distinct from free-space waves, such as those studied by Hertz in his ultra-high frequency (UHF) experiments. An example of such waves is Zenneck waves, which are surface waves that propagate along the interface of two media. Additionally, in resonant cavities, longitudinal modes represent specific standing wave patterns that result from constructive interference of waves after multiple reflections within the cavity. These modes correspond to wavelengths that are reinforced by the cavity's geometry.
